string-array.name: clover_facts
string-array.item: In a count of about 5.7 million clovers across six European countries, roughly 1 in 5,000 had four leaves — twice as common as the famous “1 in 10,000”.
A four-leaf clover isn\'t a separate species: it is usually a white clover (Trifolium repens) that grew an extra leaflet.
In 2010 researchers at the University of Georgia located the gene linked to four leaves. It is masked by the three-leaf gene, and light and temperature decide whether the fourth leaf appears.
One of the earliest written mentions dates from 1620: John Melton wrote that whoever finds “four-leaved grass” in the fields will soon find “some good thing”.
The Irish shamrock has three leaves, not four. Surveys in 1893 and 1988 found no single “true” shamrock species: people picked mostly lesser clover and white clover.
Tradition says St Patrick used the three-leaf shamrock to explain the Trinity — but the story first appears in writing only in 1726, more than a thousand years later.
By tradition, the four leaves stand for faith, hope, love and luck.
According to a legend, Eve took a four-leaf clover with her when she left the Garden of Eden, as a keepsake of Paradise.
In British and Irish folklore, carrying a four-leaf clover lets you see fairies and see through their tricks.
In Germany people give “Glücksklee” at New Year. It isn\'t a true clover but Oxalis tetraphylla, a plant whose leaves always have four lobes.
The Guinness record for the most leaves on a single clover is 63, set by Yoshiharu Watanabe in Japan in 2023.
In Japanese, white clover is called “shirotsumekusa”, “white packing grass”: in the Edo period, dried clover cushioned Dutch glassware shipped to Nagasaki.

string-array.name: preserve_steps
string-array.item: Press it as soon as possible, within a few hours. Until then keep it flat inside folded paper, not in a pocket.
If it is damp with dew or rain, blot it gently dry.
Spread the leaflets flat between two sheets of absorbent paper (blotting paper, a coffee filter or baking paper). Keep it off the book pages: ink and acidic paper can stain it.
Close it in the middle of a heavy book and add more weight on top. A flower press is even better.
Change the absorbent paper every day for the first few days, then every few days, to prevent mould and browning.
Leave it pressed somewhere dry for 1–3 weeks, until it is completely dry and stiff.
Protect it only once it is fully dry: laminate it, frame it under glass or keep it in a clear sleeve.

string-array.name: preserve_tips
string-array.item: Keep it out of direct sunlight: the green fades with time whatever you do, but light makes it faster. Lamination keeps the colour best.
Seal it only when completely dry, or it will cloud under the plastic or glass.
The quick microwave method exists, but it overheats easily and a book in the microwave is risky: the slow press is safer.
